nameStory: Ceratinops rugosus gets its scientific name from Greek 'keratos' meaning horn and 'ops' meaning face, referring to small horn-like projections on the male's head region. The species name 'rugosus' means wrinkled or rough, describing the textured surface of its body that feels like fine sandpaper when gently touched.
description: This tiny sheetweb weaver is one of New England's smallest spiders, measuring only 1-2 millimeters long - about the size of a pinhead. Its body has a distinctly rough, bumpy texture and ranges from pale yellow to light brown in color. Like other dwarf weavers, it spins delicate sheet webs close to the ground, making it easy to overlook despite being surprisingly common in suitable habitats.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small at just 1-2mm long, roughly the size of a large grain of sand or small ant

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded abdomen with a distinctly bumpy, rugose texture that feels rough like fine sandpaper

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates tiny horizontal sheet webs very close to ground level, often stretched between moss stems or small debris

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Pale yellow to light brown coloration with subtle darker mottling, often with a slightly translucent appearance

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves very slowly and deliberately, often remaining motionless for long periods when disturbed

habitat: Found in moist, sheltered microhabitats including moss beds, leaf litter, and the bases of trees in deciduous and mixed forests. Prefers areas with consistently high humidity and protection from direct sunlight, often in small depressions or crevices where moisture accumulates.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to construct their sheet webs in moss and emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most easily found on their webs. Mating occurs during warm, humid evenings.
seasonality.fall: Egg sacs are produced and adults begin to decline in numbers as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Juveniles overwinter in protected spaces deep within moss beds and leaf litter, remaining dormant until spring.

funFact: **[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Despite being smaller than many ants, Ceratinops rugosus can live for nearly two years, an exceptionally long lifespan for such a tiny spider - most insects this size live only weeks or months.
confusionNotes: Easily confused with other tiny Linyphiidae spiders, but the distinctly rough, bumpy body texture is diagnostic when viewed under magnification. Remember: 'rugosus = rough' - run your finger gently over the abdomen and you'll feel the difference.
contextualKnowledge: **[UNCERTAIN]** The extremely low observation count (only 1 recorded) in New England doesn't necessarily mean this spider is rare - it's more likely that its microscopic size makes it nearly impossible for casual observers to notice and identify without specialized equipment.
compareHints: **[UNCERTAIN CLAIMS]** Compared to its relative Ceratinops crenatus, C. rugosus has a more pronounced bumpy texture and tends to be slightly smaller overall. Both species require magnification to distinguish reliably, but the rugose texture of C. rugosus is more obvious to the touch when gently examined.
